honesty: Answers authored in-session by the coding agent. Do not relabel as OpenAI/Anthropic/Google vendor outputs.

answers.csi-03-concrete: Vertical formwork (walls/columns) is stripped when the concrete has enough strength to carry its own weight plus construction loads — not on a fixed clock alone. Follow the project specs / ACI 347 / engineer of record: many specs allow vertical form removal after concrete reaches a stated psi (often around early strength from field-cured cylinders) or after a minimum time at a given temperature. Do not strip based on calendar hours if it was cold or the mix was slow. Before stripping: confirm no honeycombing that needs repair access first, shore if the member is still load-critical, and never strip slabs/soffits on the same criteria as vertical forms (horizontal needs higher strength, often ~70% of f'c or as specified). Have the competent person / PE criteria in writing before you pull forms.
answers.osha-fall-protection: Under OSHA construction rules (29 CFR 1926.501), fall protection is generally required at 6 feet above a lower level for most walking-working surfaces. Use guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall arrest (or other allowed systems) as specified for the task. Exceptions and different trigger heights exist for some activities (e.g., scaffolds, steel erection have their own Subpart rules) — check the applicable Subpart, not only 501. Competent person must identify hazards; inspect harnesses, lanyards, and anchorage (typically 5,000 lb per worker for PFAS) before use. Do not treat 'we're only up a minute' as an exception.
answers.estimating-takeoff: Structure the takeoff by drawing set and CSI division (or your bid WBS): (1) list every quantifiable item with unit (SF, CY, LF, EA); (2) take off from plans/specs with a consistent scale and markups; (3) apply waste and productivity factors by trade; (4) price material, labor, equipment, and subs in separate columns; (5) add general conditions, bonds, insurance, contingency, and fee last. Cross-check against scope inclusions/exclusions and addenda. Level alternates and allowances separately so they do not corrupt the base bid. Historical unit costs beat generic databases when you have job-similar data. Freeze a takeoff revision tied to a drawing date before final number.
answers.billing-payapp: On an AIA-style G702/G703 package: build the Schedule of Values (SOV) as the contract breakdown (line items with scheduled value). Each period enter work completed this period and materials presently stored; prior applications carry forward. Calculate total completed & stored to date, retainage per contract, and current payment due = (total completed & stored × (1 − retainage%)) − previous payments (plus any release of retainage if allowed). Stored materials usually need invoices/bills of sale and sometimes insurance. Match percent-complete to field reality and approved COs — do not bill unapproved scope. Attach lien waivers as required by the owner/lender.
answers.scheduling-cpm: In CPM, the critical path is the longest path of dependent activities through the network — the chain with zero (or least) total float that sets the project finish date. Delay any critical activity and the finish slips one-for-one (absent acceleration). Near-critical paths with small float matter too. Build logic with real finish-to-start (and legitimate leads/lags), resource-load if needed, and update with actuals. A time impact analysis inserts a delay fragnet onto the then-current schedule to measure critical-path impact for COs/claims.
answers.closeout-punchlist: Substantial completion is the stage when the work (or a designated portion) is sufficiently complete per the contract that the owner can occupy or use it for its intended purpose — punch list items remaining are minor and do not prevent that use. The architect/owner typically issues a certificate of substantial completion; the punch list enumerates incomplete/defective items to finish before final completion. Warranties and retainage release often tie to that date. Do not call it substantial complete while life-safety, egress, or certificate-of-occupancy blockers remain open.
answers.code-egress: IBC occupant-load and exit-count rules are table-driven: typically one exit is allowed only for small loads; two exits are required once occupant load exceeds the single-exit threshold for that occupancy (commonly 49 for many business/mercantile-type situations, but verify the edition/occupancy table). Three or more exits are required at higher thresholds (e.g., 501+ and 1,001+ in common IBC tables). Exit separation, travel distance, and common-path limits also apply. Always use the adopted code edition and occupancy classification for the project — do not memorize one number for all buildings.
answers.contracts-aia-a201: Under AIA A201, the Architect interprets the Contract Documents and decides matters concerning performance in the first instance (subject to the owner-contractor dispute process). The Contractor is responsible for means and methods and for constructing per the documents; the Owner furnishes surveys/approvals as specified. RFIs should resolve genuine conflicts — not shift design responsibility improperly. Follow the claims/dispute articles for disagreements with the Architect's interpretation.
answers.insurance-bonding: A performance bond guarantees the surety will step in (or fund completion) if the bonded contractor defaults on performing the contract — protecting the obligee (usually the owner) up to the bond penal sum. It is not the same as a payment bond (labor/materials claimants) or insurance (risk transfer for covered losses). Bondability and claims processes are strict; document default properly. Owners on public work often require both performance and payment bonds.
answers.sitework-erosion: Under a SWPPP (typically CGP / local equivalent), install and maintain erosion/sediment controls before land disturbance begins — silt fence, inlet protection, stabilized construction entrance, etc., per the plan. File/obtain NOI coverage as required, train crews, inspect after rain events, and keep records. Disturb only what you can stabilize; sequence clearing with controls. Failure to install BMPs before grading is a common NOV trigger.
answers.csi-04-masonry: CMU control-joint spacing depends on wall type, reinforcement, moisture, and spec — a common rule of thumb is about every 20–25 feet horizontally for many ungrouted/lightly reinforced exterior walls, and within ~half that spacing of corners/openings, but project specs and TMS/ACI masonry guidance govern. Joints should align with openings and weak points; sealant and backer rod details matter. Do not copy a generic spacing if the structural/masonry drawings show a joint layout.
answers.osha-trenching: OSHA excavation rules (1926 Subpart P): a protective system (sloping, shoring, shielding, or engineered equivalent) is generally required for trenches 5 feet or deeper, unless the excavation is made entirely in stable rock. A competent person must inspect daily and after events that could increase hazard. At 4 feet, provide a safe means of egress (e.g., ladder within 25 feet of workers). Spoils/equipment set back from the edge; atmospheric testing when needed. Depth alone does not replace soil classification and protective-system design.
